steps.body: Every real number is either rational (a fraction a/b — its decimal terminates or repeats a block forever) or irrational (its decimal never terminates and never settles into a repeating block — π, √2, and √3 are classic examples).

widget.prompt: Sort each number: rational or irrational?

items.feedback: 16 is a perfect square (4²), so √16 = 4 exactly — rational, even though it wears a radical sign.

items.label: π
items.feedback: π's decimal never terminates or repeats — irrational.
7 isn't a perfect square, so √7 is irrational.

widget.missFeedback: Check again — a radical sign doesn't automatically mean irrational.
widget.successFeedback: All sorted — perfect-square roots are rational even though they look like radicals.

predict.prompt: A repeating decimal like 0.333… — rational or irrational?

options.label: Rational — it's a fraction in disguise

predict.reveal: Repeating is a pattern, and patterns convert to fractions — 0.333… is exactly 1/3. Irrational means no pattern EVER; endlessness alone doesn't qualify.

steps.body: A repeating decimal like 0.4545… IS rational (it equals 5/11) — it just looks messy. What makes π different is that its digits never lock into ANY repeating block, no matter how far you go — 3.14159265358979…, forever unpatterned.

explanationVariants: Rational: -3/4, √9 (=3), and 0.1010… repeating. Irrational: √11 and π.
Check each: a fraction, a perfect square, and a genuinely repeating decimal are all rational; a non-perfect-square root and π are irrational.

widget.prompt: Sort each number: rational or irrational?

items.feedback: Already a fraction of two integers — rational.
9 = 3², so √9 = 3 exactly — rational despite the radical.

items.label: 0.101010… (repeating)
items.feedback: The block "10" repeats forever — that's a genuine repeat, so it's rational (equals 10/99).

items.label: π
items.feedback: π never terminates or repeats — irrational.

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — recheck each: is it a perfect square, a genuine repeat, or neither?
widget.successFeedback: All correct — perfect squares and genuine repeats are rational; everything else here is irrational.

options.label: √37, since 37 isn't a perfect square
options.feedback: Right — 36 = 6² is a perfect square, but 37 sits just past it, unmatched.

options.label: √36, since 36 is even
options.feedback: 36 = 6² IS a perfect square — √36 = 6 exactly, rational.

options.label: Both are irrational
options.feedback: √36 = 6 exactly — that one's rational.

options.label: Neither — both are rational
options.feedback: 37 isn't a perfect square, so √37 is irrational.

explanationVariants: 64 = 8², a perfect square, so √64 = 8 exactly — rational.
8² lands exactly on 64, making this root a whole number.

options.label: Rational — exactly 8
options.feedback: Right — 8² = 64 exactly.

options.label: Irrational
options.feedback: 64 IS a perfect square (8²) — rational.

options.label: Exactly 7
options.feedback: Check by squaring: 7² = 49, which isn't 64. Since 8² = 64, the root is 8.

options.label: Approximately 8, not exact
options.feedback: It's exact — 8² = 64 precisely.

explanationVariants: This decimal keeps changing its pattern (more digits between each 3) — it never settles into ONE repeating block, so it's irrational.
A rational decimal must repeat the exact same block forever; a pattern that keeps growing is not a true repeat.

widget.prompt: Is 0.3833833383333… (the run of 3s keeps growing) rational or irrational?

options.label: Irrational — it never repeats one fixed block
options.feedback: Right — the pattern keeps changing, so no single block repeats forever.

options.label: Rational — it clearly has a pattern
options.feedback: Having SOME pattern isn't enough — a rational decimal must repeat the exact SAME block forever, and this one's block keeps growing.

options.label: Rational — all decimals with 3s and 8s repeat
options.feedback: The digits used don't decide this — whether the SAME block repeats forever does.

options.label: Can't tell without a calculator
options.feedback: You can tell from the structure alone: the growing gaps mean it never locks into one repeating block.

explanationVariants: 0.75 terminates after two digits — a clean rational decimal. √12 isn't a perfect square, π never repeats, and the last option's pattern keeps growing.
Check each: only 0.75 stops cleanly; the other three never settle into a fixed repeating block.

options.feedback: Right — 0.75 terminates after two digits.
12 isn't a perfect square (3²=9, 4²=16) — irrational.

options.label: π
options.feedback: π never terminates or repeats — irrational.

options.label: 0.12122122212222… (the pattern keeps growing)
options.feedback: The gaps between 1s keep growing — it never repeats one fixed block, so it's irrational.

hints: A rational number's decimal must either stop completely or repeat the SAME block forever.
Check each option: does it stop, does it repeat one identical block, or does it keep changing?
0.75 stops after two digits — that's the rational one. The others never settle into one repeating block, or aren't perfect squares.

steps.body: Classify by decimal behavior: stops or repeats a fixed block → rational; neither → irrational.
takeaways: Perfect-square roots and genuinely repeating decimals are rational, even when they look messy.
A decimal whose pattern keeps changing (never locking into one fixed block) is irrational.
π and non-perfect-square roots are the everyday examples of irrational numbers.
steps.teaser: Next: the number line itself has no gaps — why that matters for locating irrationals.

concept.body: Rational numbers are perfect-square roots, fractions, and decimals that terminate or repeat a fixed block. Irrational numbers are non-perfect-square roots and decimals (like π) that never terminate or repeat.

explanationVariants: 25 = 5², a perfect square, so √25 = 5 exactly — rational.
5² lands exactly on 25, making this root a whole number.

options.label: Rational — exactly 5
options.feedback: Right — 5² = 25 exactly.

options.label: Irrational
options.feedback: 25 IS a perfect square (5²) — rational.

options.label: Exactly 4
options.feedback: Check by squaring: 4² = 16, which isn't 25. Since 5² = 25, the root is 5.

options.label: Approximately 5, not exact
options.feedback: It's exact — 5² = 25 precisely.
